In 1987 Fisher-Price sold a video camera for kids that recorded onto ordinary audio cassettes. It was the PXL 2000, it cost about $100, and it stayed on the market for roughly a year.



Getting pictures onto a cassette meant running the tape far faster than any cassette deck would, close to nine times normal speed, so a 90 minute high-bias tape held about eleven minutes of video and sound. The picture was black and white, small, soft and grainy, and it ran on six AA batteries.



It flopped as a toy and then found a second life. Experimental filmmakers and artists took to the camera for exactly the qualities that made it a bad toy, and the look got its own name, Pixelvision. Films shot on it ended up in festivals and galleries, which must have surprised Fisher-Price.



The clip is a busker in Bratislava's old town through the simulated PXL 2000 on a black and white set, then normal video on the same set.
